intro: Listen to a talk in a biology class.
talk: So, for the first half of the twentieth century, biologists believed that ordinary animal cells, given the right nutrients, could keep dividing in a dish forever. That belief came largely from a French surgeon, Alexis Carrel, who claimed he'd kept chicken heart cells growing for more than thirty years. In nineteen sixty-one, a researcher named Leonard Hayflick showed it wasn't true. Human fetal cells in his cultures divided roughly forty to sixty times, and then they just stopped. They didn't die; they entered a permanent retirement we call senescence. That ceiling became known as the Hayflick limit. But what was counting the divisions? The answer lies at the tips of our chromosomes, in structures called telomeres. A telomere is a short DNA sequence repeated over a thousand times, a bit like the plastic cap on a shoelace. Now, here's the mechanism, in three steps. First, every time a cell copies its DNA, the copying machinery can't quite reach the very end of the strand. Second, so with each division, the telomere gets shorter. Third, once it falls below a critical length, the cell reads that as damage and stops dividing. So why don't the cells that make sperm and eggs run out? They use an enzyme called telomerase, which rebuilds the caps. And cancer cells? Roughly eighty-five to ninety percent of them switch telomerase back on, which is partly why they divide indefinitely. As for Carrel's chicken cells? Most likely, fresh cells were added each time the cultures were fed.

options: Why normal human cells stop dividing after a limited number of divisions
How cancer cells repair the damaged ends of their DNA before each new division
Why chicken cells survive longer in culture than human cells
How telomerase was first discovered in reproductive cells
questions.explanation: The professor explains the Hayflick limit and how shrinking telomeres cause normal cells to stop dividing.

questions.explanation: The professor says Hayflick's human fetal cells divided roughly forty to sixty times and then entered senescence.

options: Both stop dividing once their telomeres reach a critical length.
Both copy the very ends of their DNA without any loss.
Both use telomerase to rebuild the ends of their chromosomes.
Both were first grown in Carrel's long-term cultures.
questions.explanation: The professor says reproductive cells use telomerase to rebuild telomeres and that most cancer cells switch telomerase back on.

questions.prompt: What does the professor imply about Carrel's chicken heart cells?
options: They lacked telomeres and therefore never aged.
They proved that some animal cells really are immortal.
They used telomerase in the same way cancer cells do.
The original cells probably never divided indefinitely.
questions.explanation: The professor suggests fresh cells were added at each feeding, so the original cells were not truly immortal.

intro: Listen to a talk in a biology class.
talk: Okay, here's a strange fact about your cells. Inside almost every one are hundreds, sometimes thousands, of mitochondria, the structures that produce most of the cell's usable energy. And mitochondria have their own DNA. Just thirty-seven genes in humans, but it's separate from the DNA in the nucleus, and it's arranged in a circular loop, the way bacterial DNA is. Why would that be? The explanation is called endosymbiotic theory. The modern version was laid out by Lynn Margulis in nineteen sixty-seven, and the idea is that mitochondria were once free-living bacteria. There were three stages. First, probably more than a billion and a half years ago, a larger cell engulfed a smaller bacterium, but instead of digesting it, kept it alive inside. Second, the two became partners: the bacterium used oxygen to release energy, and the host provided shelter and raw materials. Third, over countless generations, most of the bacterium's genes moved into the host's nucleus, so it could no longer live independently. Now, chloroplasts in plants have the same story, except their ancestors were cyanobacteria, bacteria that could photosynthesize. And the evidence lines up for both: double membranes, circular DNA, and ribosomes that resemble bacterial ones rather than ours. Here's what's interesting, though. Margulis's paper was reportedly rejected by about fifteen journals, and many biologists dismissed it as fanciful. Today, it's in every introductory textbook. The debate now isn't whether it happened, but exactly when, and what kind of cell did the swallowing.

options: How mitochondria convert oxygen into energy for the nucleus
The theory that mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from bacteria
Why bacterial DNA is arranged in a circular loop
How early cyanobacteria first developed the ability to photosynthesize
questions.explanation: The lecturer explains endosymbiotic theory, the idea that mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living bacteria.

options: It contains more genes than the DNA in the nucleus.
It is stored inside the nucleus with the cell's other DNA.

It is identical in the cells of plants and animals.
questions.explanation: The lecturer notes that mitochondrial DNA is separate from nuclear DNA and is arranged in a circular loop like bacterial DNA.

options: A larger cell engulfed a bacterium without digesting it.
The bacterium supplied energy in exchange for shelter.

questions.explanation: The third stage the lecturer describes is the movement of most of the bacterium's genes into the host's nucleus.

options: To contrast the theory's early reception with its current acceptance
To suggest that the evidence for the theory is still weak
To explain why chloroplasts were studied long before mitochondria were
To show that the timing of the theory is still being debated
questions.explanation: The lecturer contrasts the early rejections with the fact that the theory is now in every introductory textbook.

intro: Listen to a talk in an ecology class.
talk: Here's a pattern naturalists noticed long before anyone explained it. Big islands have more species than small ones, and islands close to a mainland have more species than remote ones. In the nineteen sixties, two ecologists, Robert MacArthur and E. O. Wilson, turned that observation into a theory. Their key idea was that an island's species count reflects a balance between two processes: immigration, new species arriving, and extinction, species already there dying out. Now, distance mainly affects immigration. A bird or seed is far likelier to reach an island ten kilometers offshore than one a thousand kilometers out. Size mainly affects extinction, because small islands support small populations, and small populations are easily wiped out by a storm or a disease. So species numbers settle at an equilibrium. Then Wilson and his student Daniel Simberloff tested this directly. They chose tiny mangrove islands off the Florida Keys, each only about eleven to twenty-five meters across, covered them with tents, and fumigated them to remove every insect and spider. Within about a year, the islands had been recolonized, and here's the striking part: each one returned to roughly its original number of species, with the closest island again ending up with the most. But, and this is important, they weren't the same species as before. The total stayed about the same while the membership changed. Today, the theory is applied to mountaintops, lakes, and especially forest patches cut off by farms and roads, which behave a lot like islands.

options: An experiment showing that insects tend to avoid the smallest mangrove islands
Why species on remote islands are more likely to become extinct
A theory explaining how island size and distance affect species numbers
How forest patches differ from ocean islands in their species
questions.explanation: The professor presents MacArthur and Wilson's theory of how immigration and extinction set the number of species on islands.

options: Small islands are harder for birds and seeds to reach.

Small islands have small populations that die out more easily.
questions.explanation: The professor says size mainly affects extinction because small islands support small, vulnerable populations.

options: Their species totals returned, but the species themselves were different.
They regained exactly the same species they had before fumigation.
The most distant islands ended up with more species than the closer ones.
Their species totals stayed far below their original levels.
questions.explanation: The professor says each island returned to roughly its original number of species, but not the same species as before.

options: It will gradually be recolonized by exactly the same species it lost.

questions.explanation: The professor says forest patches behave like islands, so the theory's factors of size and distance should apply to them.

intro: Listen to a talk in an ecology class.
talk: What happens to land after a disaster wipes it clean? Ecologists call the process succession, the gradual change in which species occupy a place over time. There are two kinds. Primary succession starts from bare rock or fresh lava, where there's no soil at all. The first arrivals, the pioneer species, are often lichens, which can cling to rock and slowly break it down. Then mosses take hold, then grasses, then shrubs, and eventually trees. That can take centuries, because the soil has to be built almost from nothing. Secondary succession is faster. It follows a fire, a flood, or an abandoned farm, where the soil survives, along with seeds and roots buried in it. An old field in New England, for instance, can go from weeds to a young pine forest in about thirty years. Now, for much of the twentieth century, ecologists, following Frederic Clements, described this as an orderly march toward a single stable endpoint, the climax community, like an organism growing up. But the eruption of Mount Saint Helens in nineteen eighty challenged that picture. Recovery didn't follow one script. In places, gophers that had survived underground churned up buried soil, and plants sprang up almost immediately. Elsewhere, a single lupine seed blown in started a patch that enriched the soil for others. So today ecologists see succession as far more variable, shaped by chance, by which survivors remained, and by repeated disturbance. It's less a staircase than a branching set of possible paths.

options: Why lichens are the first species to grow on fresh lava
How the eruption of Mount Saint Helens destroyed a stable, mature climax forest
Why abandoned farms recover more slowly than lava fields
How plant communities recover after disturbance and how that view changed
questions.explanation: The professor describes primary and secondary succession and explains how ecologists' view of the process has changed.

options: They begin breaking down bare rock before other plants arrive.
They replace the mosses and grasses that grow on the rock first.
They survive underground and sprout again after a fire.
They form the stable final stage of the plant community.
questions.explanation: The professor says lichens are pioneer species that cling to rock and slowly break it down.

Soil, seeds, and roots remain in place after the disturbance.

options: To show that animals always recover before plants after an eruption
To illustrate the orderly stages of Clements's climax model
To show that recovery depended on chance survivors and arrivals
To explain why primary succession takes many centuries
questions.explanation: These cases show that recovery at Mount Saint Helens followed different paths depending on what happened to survive or arrive.

intro: Listen to a talk in a zoology class.
talk: What do we mean when we say an animal hibernates? It's more than a long sleep. Hibernation is a state in which an animal deliberately lowers its metabolism, its body temperature, and its heart rate to survive a season when food is scarce. Let's compare two examples. The first is the arctic ground squirrel of Alaska. Its normal body temperature is around thirty-seven degrees Celsius, like ours. In hibernation, it falls below zero, to about minus three degrees, the lowest ever recorded in a mammal, and yet its blood doesn't freeze. Its heart slows from about two hundred beats a minute to a few. Now, here's the odd part. Every two or three weeks, the squirrel rewarms itself to normal temperature for about a day, then cools down again. These arousals burn most of its winter energy, and nobody's sure why they're needed, though one idea is that the brain and immune system need maintenance. The second example is the black bear. A bear's temperature drops only a few degrees, to around thirty-two or thirty-three. So for decades, many biologists said bears weren't true hibernators; they just entered a deep winter sleep. But when researchers measured bear metabolism directly, they found it falls to about a quarter of the normal rate, a drop far bigger than the small temperature change would predict. Bears also go months without eating or drinking, recycling their waste into protein. So the old distinction is mostly gone. Bears are hibernators, just at a warmer temperature.

options: Two patterns of hibernation and how scientists classify them

How bears recycle waste to survive months without food
Why some animals sleep through winter instead of hibernating
questions.explanation: The lecturer compares hibernation in the arctic ground squirrel and the black bear and explains why bears are now considered hibernators.

questions.explanation: The lecturer says the squirrel's temperature falls to about minus three degrees without its blood freezing.

The squirrel goes all winter without rewarming, unlike the bear.
The squirrel's temperature falls much further than the bear's does.
The bear rewarms itself every few weeks, unlike the squirrel.
questions.explanation: The squirrel cools to about minus three degrees, while the bear drops only to around thirty-two or thirty-three.

questions.prompt: Why does the lecturer mention that bear metabolism falls to about a quarter of normal?
options: To show that bears save more energy than ground squirrels
To explain why bears must wake up every few weeks
To support the view that bears simply sleep deeply
To explain why bears are now considered true hibernators
questions.explanation: The large metabolic drop is the evidence that led biologists to abandon the claim that bears only sleep deeply.

intro: Listen to a talk on a podcast about animal behavior.
talk: Welcome back. Today's puzzle is one of nature's great navigation feats. A Pacific salmon hatches in a small stream, swims down to the ocean, and spends two to five years there, traveling thousands of kilometers. Then it returns, often to the exact stream where it hatched. How? In the nineteen forties, a biologist named Arthur Hasler had an idea while hiking. He came around a bend and recognized the smell of a waterfall from his childhood. Maybe salmon, he thought, do the same thing. Each stream has its own chemical signature. So his hypothesis worked in two steps. First, young salmon memorize the smell of their home stream before they leave, a process called imprinting. Second, as adults, they follow that smell upstream, choosing the right branch at each fork. And experiments supported it. When Hasler's team plugged the noses of returning salmon, the fish chose branches almost at random. Later, they raised young fish in water containing an artificial chemical, morpholine, and released them. Years later, those fish were drawn to streams that had been scented with morpholine. But smell has a limit. In the open ocean, far from the coast, there's no river odor to follow. So how do they find the right coastline? The current answer is magnetism. Studies of sockeye salmon suggest they also imprint on the magnetic field near the river mouth. So the picture now is a two-stage journey: a magnetic map for the ocean, and smell for the final stretch.

options: How young salmon learn to survive in the open ocean
How salmon find their way back to the streams where they hatched
Why salmon migrate farther than most other kinds of fish
How natural chemicals in streams affect the growth of young salmon
questions.explanation: The host explains the evidence that salmon use smell and magnetism to return to their home streams.

questions.explanation: The host says Hasler recognized the smell of a waterfall from his childhood and wondered if salmon did the same.

They use smell to imprint and magnetism to choose at each fork.

questions.explanation: The host describes a magnetic map for the open ocean and smell for the final stretch upstream.

options: To describe an experiment showing that salmon imprint on a stream's odor
To explain why salmon avoid streams that are polluted by artificial chemicals
To show that plugging the noses of salmon changed their behavior
To identify the chemical that gives each stream its signature
questions.explanation: Fish raised in morpholine later chose streams scented with it, supporting the idea that salmon imprint on odors.

intro: Listen to a talk in a botany class.
talk: Okay, photosynthesis has a built-in flaw. The enzyme that captures carbon dioxide, called rubisco, is probably the most abundant protein on Earth, but it's surprisingly sloppy. It sometimes grabs oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, and that mistake, called photorespiration, wastes energy. It gets worse when it's hot and dry, because in heat, plants close their stomata, the tiny pores on their leaves, to save water. That means less carbon dioxide gets in, so rubisco grabs oxygen more often. Some plants have evolved two main workarounds. The first is C4 photosynthesis, used by corn and sugarcane. These plants separate the work in space. Cells near the leaf surface capture carbon dioxide using a different enzyme, one that ignores oxygen, and pack it into a four-carbon molecule. That's where the name comes from. Then it's shuttled to cells deeper inside the leaf, where the carbon dioxide is released at high concentration, right next to rubisco. The second is CAM, used by cacti and pineapples. These plants separate the work in time. They open their stomata only at night, when it's cool, store the carbon dioxide as an acid, and then close up during the day and use that stored carbon for photosynthesis. You might expect such systems to be common. They're not. Only about three percent of plant species use C4. And yet, those few species account for nearly a quarter of all the photosynthesis on land. Even more surprising, C4 didn't evolve once. It appeared independently more than sixty times.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why rubisco is the most abundant protein on Earth
How cacti and pineapples store water in their stems during the day
Two ways that plants reduce a weakness of the enzyme rubisco
Why corn grows faster than most other food crops
questions.explanation: The professor explains how C4 and CAM photosynthesis help plants avoid rubisco's tendency to grab oxygen.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, why does photorespiration increase in hot, dry conditions?
options: Rubisco breaks down more quickly at high temperatures.
Plants open their stomata, so more oxygen enters.
Heat causes plants to produce more four-carbon molecules.
Plants close their stomata, so less carbon dioxide enters.
questions.explanation: The professor says plants close their stomata to save water, so less carbon dioxide gets in and rubisco grabs oxygen more often.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between C4 plants and CAM plants?
options: C4 plants separate the steps in space, and CAM plants in time.
C4 plants separate the steps in time, and CAM plants in space.
C4 plants open their stomata at night, and CAM plants by day.
C4 plants rely on rubisco, while CAM plants avoid it entirely.
questions.explanation: The professor says C4 plants divide the work between different cells, while CAM plants divide it between night and day.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor point out that C4 photosynthesis evolved more than sixty times?
options: To explain why only three percent of plant species use the pathway
To emphasize how strongly the pathway has been favored by evolution
To suggest that CAM plants originally evolved from C4 plants
To show that corn and sugarcane are not closely related plants
questions.explanation: The professor presents the repeated independent evolution of C4 as a surprising sign of how advantageous the pathway is.

intro: Listen to a talk in a botany class.
talk: Charles Darwin called the Venus flytrap one of the most wonderful plants in the world. It grows wild only in a small area of the Carolinas, in boggy soil that's very poor in nitrogen. So it gets nitrogen another way: by catching insects. Compare it with a more common strategy, the pitcher plant. A pitcher plant is passive. Its leaves form a deep, slippery tube, often with sweet nectar near the rim. Insects fall in, can't climb out, and drown. Nothing moves. The flytrap, on the other hand, actively snaps shut. Each lobe of the trap has three tiny trigger hairs. Here's the clever part: touching one hair once does nothing. The trap closes only if hairs are touched twice within about twenty seconds. In effect, the plant counts. So a raindrop, which touches just once, doesn't waste a closure. After two touches, the trap shuts in about a tenth of a second. And if the insect keeps struggling and triggers the hairs three more times, so five in total, the trap seals tightly and begins releasing digestive enzymes. If nothing struggles, it reopens in a day or so. How does a plant without muscles move that fast? Botanists long assumed it was mainly water rushing between cells. Water plays a role, but in two thousand five, physicists showed the key is the shape of the leaf. The lobes curve outward, under tension, and when triggered, they suddenly flip to curve inward, like a contact lens popping inside out.

options: Why pitcher plants are more common than Venus flytraps
How carnivorous plants obtain water in boggy soil
Why Darwin studied carnivorous plants in the Carolinas
How the Venus flytrap detects and captures its prey
questions.explanation: The lecturer explains how the flytrap counts touches, closes, digests prey, and moves so quickly.

Its leaves snap shut when trigger hairs are touched.

questions.explanation: The lecturer describes the pitcher plant as passive: insects fall into a slippery tube and drown.

options: The trap reopens to release the struggling insect within about a day.
The trap seals tightly and starts releasing digestive enzymes.
The trap closes for the first time in a tenth of a second.
The trap fills with fluid that slowly drowns the insect.
questions.explanation: The lecturer says three more touches, five in total, cause the trap to seal and begin releasing enzymes.

options: To show how water rushes between the cells of the trap
To compare the thinness of the trap's lobes with that of a clear lens
To illustrate how the curved lobes suddenly reverse their shape
To explain how the trap counts the number of touches
questions.explanation: The contact lens popping inside out illustrates the lobes flipping from curving outward to curving inward.

intro: Listen to a talk in a physiology class.
talk: If you've eaten chicken, you've noticed the breast meat is white and the leg meat dark. That's a great introduction to muscle fiber types. Skeletal muscle contains two broad kinds of fibers. Type one, or slow-twitch fibers, contract relatively slowly, but they can keep going for hours. They're packed with mitochondria and with a red, oxygen-storing protein called myoglobin, which is what makes them dark. Type two, or fast-twitch fibers, contract two or three times faster and more forcefully, but they rely mainly on energy sources that don't need oxygen, so they tire within seconds to minutes. They have less myoglobin, so they look pale. Now, back to the chicken. A chicken walks around all day, so its legs are rich in slow-twitch fibers. But it flies only in short, explosive bursts to escape danger, so its breast is mostly fast-twitch. Compare that with a duck or a goose. Those birds migrate long distances, and sure enough, their breast meat is dark. Humans show a similar pattern. In the calf muscles of elite marathon runners, as much as eighty percent of fibers may be slow-twitch, while top sprinters often have the reverse. So, does training create these differences? But the evidence suggests your basic proportion is largely inherited. Training improves how well each fiber works, and it can shift fast fibers from one subtype to another, but turning fast fibers into slow ones happens only to a limited degree. Champions are partly made, and partly born.

options: The properties of two types of muscle fibers and what shapes them
Why white chicken breast meat is healthier to eat than dark leg meat
How marathon runners train to build fast-twitch fibers
Why ducks can fly much longer distances than chickens
questions.explanation: The professor contrasts slow-twitch and fast-twitch fibers and discusses whether training or inheritance determines their proportions.

options: They contain fewer mitochondria than fast fibers.
They contain a red protein that stores oxygen.
They contract more forcefully than other fibers.
They rely on energy that does not require oxygen.
questions.explanation: The professor says slow-twitch fibers are dark because they are packed with myoglobin, a red oxygen-storing protein.

options: Chickens fly long distances, so their breast muscles contain no myoglobin.
Ducks walk more than chickens, so they use their breasts less.
Ducks fly long distances, so their breast muscles are mostly slow-twitch.
Ducks fly in short bursts, so their breasts are mostly fast-twitch.
questions.explanation: Migrating ducks need endurance flight muscles, which are slow-twitch and dark, while chickens fly only in short bursts.

options: It is the main reason that elite sprinters have mostly fast-twitch fibers.
It has no measurable effect on any type of muscle fiber.
It converts most fast fibers into slow ones over time.
It improves fiber performance but changes the basic mix only slightly.
questions.explanation: The professor says the basic proportion is largely inherited and training shifts fast fibers to slow ones only to a limited degree.

intro: Listen to a talk on a podcast about the human body.
talk: Hi everyone, welcome back. Today: how does a seal hold its breath for over an hour? The Weddell seal of Antarctica regularly dives to a few hundred meters, and its record dives last more than eighty minutes and reach about six hundred meters deep. A trained human diver might manage a few minutes. You'd probably guess the seal takes a huge breath. Actually, it does the opposite. It breathes out before diving. Its lungs collapse under the pressure, which keeps nitrogen from dissolving into its blood and protects it from the bends. So where's its oxygen? Mostly in the blood and muscles. A seal has roughly twice as much blood per kilogram as we do, and its muscles are so full of myoglobin they look almost black. Then, once it submerges, a set of responses called the diving reflex kicks in, in three steps. First, its heart rate drops sharply, sometimes to a small fraction of its resting rate. Second, blood vessels to the skin, gut, and muscles constrict, so the limited oxygen goes mainly to the brain and heart. Third, the spleen contracts, squeezing a reserve of red blood cells into circulation. Here's what surprised me. Humans have this reflex too, just a weaker version. Put your face in cold water, and your heart rate slows within seconds. And among the Bajau people of Southeast Asia, who've dived for food for generations, researchers found spleens about fifty percent larger than those of their non-diving neighbors.

options: Why seals breathe in deeply before beginning a long dive
How seals and other mammals survive long periods underwater
How the Bajau people learned to dive by watching seals
Why nitrogen in the blood causes the bends in human divers
questions.explanation: The host explains how the Weddell seal stores oxygen and uses the diving reflex, and notes that humans share a weaker version.

questions.prompt: According to the host, why does a Weddell seal breathe out before diving?
options: Empty lungs allow it to store much more oxygen in its blood and muscles.
Breathing out slows its heart rate before it submerges.
Its collapsed lungs keep nitrogen from dissolving into its blood.
Exhaling makes its spleen release extra red blood cells.
questions.explanation: The host says the seal's lungs collapse, which prevents nitrogen from dissolving into the blood and causing the bends.

questions.prompt: Which response does the host describe as the final step of the diving reflex?
options: The heart rate drops to a fraction of its resting level.
Blood vessels to the skin and gut begin to narrow.
The lungs collapse and push out the remaining air.
The spleen releases stored red blood cells into the blood.
questions.explanation: The host lists a slower heart rate first, narrowed blood vessels second, and the spleen contracting third.

questions.prompt: Why does the host mention the Bajau people?
options: To show that humans can also have diving adaptations
To compare the size of their lungs with a seal's lungs
To explain where the diving reflex was first discovered
To show that some humans can dive as deeply as seals
questions.explanation: The Bajau's enlarged spleens illustrate that humans have a version of the same adaptations seen in seals.

intro: Listen to a talk in a medicine class.
talk: Vaccination didn't start in a laboratory. It started with a risky practice called variolation. For centuries, in parts of Asia and Africa, people deliberately infected healthy individuals with material from a smallpox sore, usually scratched into the skin. This generally produced a milder case, followed by lifelong immunity. It wasn't safe, though. About one or two percent of variolated people died, compared with roughly thirty percent of those who caught smallpox naturally. The practice reached England in seventeen twenty-one, largely through Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, who'd seen it in Constantinople. Then came the decisive step. Country people had long noticed that milkmaids who caught cowpox, a mild disease from cattle, seemed never to get smallpox. In seventeen ninety-six, the English doctor Edward Jenner tested this. He took material from a cowpox sore on a milkmaid's hand and inoculated an eight-year-old boy, James Phipps. Weeks later, he exposed the boy to smallpox. Nothing happened. The boy was protected without ever having had smallpox itself. That's where our word vaccine comes from: vacca is Latin for cow. Now, textbooks often call Jenner the inventor of vaccination. That's not quite fair. In seventeen seventy-four, twenty-two years earlier, a farmer named Benjamin Jesty had inoculated his wife and two sons with cowpox during an outbreak. What Jenner did differently was test the idea deliberately, document it, and publish it, so others could repeat it. And that's what eventually led to smallpox being declared eradicated in nineteen eighty.

options: Why variolation was safer than catching smallpox naturally

intro: Listen to a talk in a medicine class.
talk: Until the nineteen eighties, medical students learned that stomach ulcers were caused by stress, spicy food, and too much acid. Patients were told to relax and take antacids, and the ulcers often returned. Doctors also assumed the stomach was sterile. With a pH of around one or two, it seemed far too acidic for bacteria to survive. Then, in Perth, Australia, a pathologist named Robin Warren began noticing curved bacteria in stomach tissue samples, almost always where the lining was inflamed. A young doctor, Barry Marshall, joined him to test whether the bacteria caused it. At first, they couldn't grow the bacteria in the lab. Culture plates were routinely thrown out after two days. But over the Easter holiday in nineteen eighty-two, some plates were left for five days, and finally there were colonies. The bacterium simply grew slowly. It was later named Helicobacter pylori. How does it survive the acid? It burrows into the mucus lining the stomach and produces an enzyme, urease, that generates ammonia, which neutralizes the acid around it. Few experts believed them, so in nineteen eighty-four, Marshall drank a culture of the bacteria himself. Within about a week he was vomiting, and a biopsy showed severe inflammation. Eventually, the evidence won, ulcers became curable with antibiotics, and in two thousand five, the two men shared the Nobel Prize. One caution, though: the bacterium isn't the whole story. Most infected people never develop an ulcer, and painkillers like aspirin cause many ulcers on their own.

How a bacterium was identified as a major cause of stomach ulcers

intro: Listen to a talk in a geology class.
talk: In nineteen twelve, the German meteorologist Alfred Wegener proposed something outrageous: that the continents had once been joined in a single landmass and had since drifted apart. He called that supercontinent Pangaea. His evidence was threefold. First, the coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like puzzle pieces. Second, fossils of the same species turned up on continents now separated by oceans. The best example is Mesosaurus, a small reptile that lived in fresh water, found in both Brazil and southern Africa. It didn't swim the Atlantic. Third, ancient glaciers had left traces in now-tropical places like India. Yet geologists rejected him for decades, because he couldn't explain how it happened. He suggested continents plowed through the ocean floor, pushed by forces linked to Earth's rotation, which physicists showed were far too weak. After the Second World War, the ocean floor was mapped. Researchers found a mountain range down the middle of the Atlantic, with a rift valley along its center. And when ships towed magnetic instruments across it, they found stripes of rock magnetized in alternating directions, a record of Earth's magnetic field flipping over time. Crucially, the stripes were symmetrical on both sides of the ridge. New sea floor was forming at the ridge and spreading outward, a few centimeters a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. So Wegener was right that continents move, but wrong about how. They don't plow through the sea floor; they ride along with it, as parts of larger plates.

options: How the idea of drifting continents was rejected and later revised
How Wegener measured the speed at which the continents drifted apart
Why the coastlines of Africa and South America match
How Earth's magnetic field created the Atlantic Ocean
questions.explanation: The lecturer explains Wegener's evidence, why his theory was rejected, and how sea-floor spreading later confirmed and revised it.

intro: Listen to a talk in a geology class.
talk: How do geologists know a rock is, say, two billion years old? The answer is radiometric dating, and it depends on one key fact. Radioactive atoms break down at a steady, predictable rate, unaffected by heat, pressure, or chemistry. We describe that rate by the half-life, the time it takes for half the atoms in a sample to decay. The most famous method, carbon dating, is also the most misunderstood. Carbon fourteen has a half-life of about five thousand seven hundred thirty years. Living things absorb it constantly, and when they die, the clock starts. But after about fifty thousand years, so little remains that it can't be measured. So carbon dating is useless for dinosaurs, which died out sixty-six million years ago. For really old rocks, geologists use uranium, and the favorite tool is a tiny crystal called zircon. Here's how it works. First, when a zircon crystal forms from cooling magma, it readily takes uranium into its structure but almost completely rejects lead. Second, over time, uranium two thirty-eight decays into lead, with a half-life of about four and a half billion years. Third, a geologist measures the ratio of lead to uranium in the crystal. Since the crystal started with essentially no lead, all the lead must have come from decay. Zircons from Western Australia have been dated this way to about four point four billion years, among Earth's oldest materials. And dinosaur bones? They're dated indirectly, by dating volcanic ash layers above and below them.

options: Why carbon dating is the most accurate method for old rocks
How scientists use radioactive decay to find the ages of materials
How zircon crystals form when magma slowly cools beneath the surface
Why dinosaur bones contain more carbon than volcanic rocks do
questions.explanation: The professor explains half-lives and compares carbon dating with uranium-lead dating of zircon.

options: Dinosaur bones contain uranium instead of carbon fourteen.
Carbon fourteen decays much faster under great heat and pressure underground.

Dinosaurs absorbed very little carbon fourteen while alive.
questions.explanation: The professor says carbon fourteen becomes unmeasurable after about fifty thousand years, far less than sixty-six million.

options: The crystal absorbed lead from magma at a steady, predictable rate.

The crystal rejected uranium when it formed, so its uranium came later.
The crystal rejected lead when it formed, so its lead came from decay.
questions.explanation: Zircon takes in uranium but rejects lead as it forms, so any lead present must come from uranium decay.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about the volcanic ash layers mentioned at the end?
options: They can be dated with long-lived isotopes such as uranium.
They contain enough carbon fourteen to be dated directly.

They formed at exactly the same time as the dinosaur bones.
questions.explanation: Since carbon dating fails for such ages, the ash layers must be dated with long half-life methods like the uranium method.

intro: Listen to a talk on a podcast about ocean science.
talk: Welcome back. Today's topic is the tide. Most coastlines get two high tides and two low tides a day, and each high tide arrives about fifty minutes later than the day before. That's a clue the Moon is involved, because the Moon also rises about fifty minutes later each day. Now, the Moon's gravity pulls on the ocean, creating a bulge of water on the side of Earth facing it. But there's also a second bulge on the opposite side, facing away. Why? Because the Moon pulls hardest on the near side, less on Earth's center, and least on the far side. So the far-side water is essentially left behind. Earth rotates through both bulges, giving two high tides. What about the Sun? Its pull on Earth is much stronger than the Moon's, yet its effect on tides is only about half as large. That's because tides depend on the difference in pull from one side of Earth to the other, and that difference fades quickly with distance. When the Sun, Moon, and Earth line up, at new moon and full moon, their effects add together, giving extra-high spring tides. That has nothing to do with the season. At half moon, they work against each other, producing weaker neap tides. In the open ocean, the tide is often under a meter. But in Canada's Bay of Fundy it can reach sixteen meters, because water sloshes back and forth in the bay at nearly the same rhythm as the tide itself.

options: Why the Moon rises fifty minutes later each day
Why the Sun's gravity is stronger than the Moon's
What causes tides and why their size varies
Why the Bay of Fundy has only two tides a day
questions.explanation: The host explains how the Moon and Sun produce tides and why spring tides, neap tides, and local tides differ in size.

questions.prompt: According to the host, why is there a bulge of water on the side of Earth facing away from the Moon?
options: The Sun pulls that water toward itself during the night.
The Moon pulls the far-side water more strongly than the near side.
Earth's rotation flings that water outward toward space.
The Moon pulls the far-side water less than it pulls Earth's center.
questions.explanation: The host says the Moon pulls least on the far side, so that water is left behind as Earth's center is pulled away.

options: Spring tides come when the Sun and Moon align, neap tides at half moon.
Spring tides occur only in spring, and neap tides during the rest of the year.
Spring tides occur at half moon, and neap tides at the new and full moon.
Spring tides are caused by the Sun, and neap tides are caused by the Moon.
questions.explanation: Spring tides come when the Sun, Moon, and Earth line up; neap tides come at half moon when their effects work against each other.

options: To show that tides in the open ocean are usually less than a meter high
To show how a coastline's shape can greatly increase a tide's height
To show where spring tides were first measured and named
To give an example of a place that has only one tide a day
questions.explanation: The bay's tide reaches sixteen meters because its water sloshes at nearly the same rhythm as the tide.

intro: Listen to a talk in an oceanography class.
talk: In nineteen seventy-seven, geologists took the submersible Alvin down about two and a half kilometers to a volcanic ridge near the Galápagos Islands. They were looking for hot springs on the sea floor, and they found them. What they didn't expect was life: clams the size of dinner plates, mussels, and, most striking, giant tube worms, some nearly two meters long, with bright red plumes. With no biologists aboard, they reportedly preserved specimens in vodka. This was a shock, because at that depth there's no sunlight, and nearly every food chain we knew began with photosynthesis. So what were these animals eating? The answer is chemosynthesis. The vent water is loaded with hydrogen sulfide, the gas that smells like rotten eggs. Certain bacteria get energy by breaking it down, and they use that energy to build sugars from carbon dioxide, the way plants use sunlight. Tube worms are remarkable. An adult has no mouth and no gut at all. Instead, it houses billions of these bacteria inside its body. Its red plume, colored by a special hemoglobin, absorbs sulfide and oxygen from the water and delivers them to the bacteria, which in turn feed the worm. Two years later, explorers found even hotter vents, called black smokers, pouring out water at over three hundred fifty degrees Celsius. Now, it's often said that vent life is completely independent of the Sun. That's not quite right. The bacteria need oxygen, and that oxygen originally came from photosynthesis near the surface.

How black smokers heat seawater to very high temperatures
Why giant tube worms have plumes that are bright red
How animals at deep-sea vents survive without sunlight
questions.explanation: The professor explains that vent communities depend on chemosynthetic bacteria rather than on photosynthesis.

options: It is correct, since chemosynthesis requires no oxygen of any kind.
It is misleading, since a small amount of sunlight still reaches the deepest vents.

It is accurate only for the black smokers that were found later.
questions.explanation: The professor says the claim is not quite right because the bacteria need oxygen produced by photosynthesis at the surface.

intro: Listen to a talk in a meteorology class.
talk: So, what's actually happening in a lightning strike? It starts with a separation of electric charge inside a thunderstorm cloud. Strong updrafts carry droplets high up, where they freeze. Mid-cloud, small ice crystals rising in the updraft collide with heavier pellets of soft hail called graupel. In those collisions, the ice crystals usually end up positively charged and get carried to the top of the cloud, while the graupel becomes negatively charged and sinks toward the bottom. So the base of the cloud becomes strongly negative. Air is normally a good insulator, so the charge builds until it overcomes that resistance. The strike itself happens in stages. First, a faint channel of charged air, called a stepped leader, zigzags down from the cloud in jumps of about fifty meters. Second, as it nears the ground, tall objects, a tree, a tower, send up a streamer of positive charge to meet it. Third, once they connect, a huge current surges through the channel. That's the return stroke, and it's the bright flash you actually see. Interestingly, it travels upward, from ground to cloud, too fast for our eyes to tell. The return stroke heats the air to around thirty thousand degrees Celsius, about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun. The air expands so violently that it creates a shock wave: thunder. And the saying that lightning never strikes the same place twice is simply false. The Empire State Building gets hit about twenty times a year.
