options: How electric charge builds up in storms and produces lightning
Why tall buildings are struck by lightning more often than trees
How thunder travels faster than the flash of lightning
Why graupel forms only in the middle of storm clouds
questions.explanation: The professor explains charge separation in thunderclouds and the stages of a lightning strike.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, what happens when ice crystals collide with graupel?
options: The crystals gain negative charge and sink to the cloud base.
The crystals gain positive charge and are carried upward.
The graupel gains positive charge and rises to the top.
The graupel melts and releases its charge as rain.
questions.explanation: The professor says the ice crystals become positively charged and are carried to the top of the cloud.

questions.prompt: Which event occurs immediately before the return stroke?
options: The stepped leader zigzags upward in jumps from the ground to the cloud.
A shock wave from the heated air produces the sound of thunder.
A streamer rising from the ground connects with the stepped leader.
The ice crystals rise and leave the top of the cloud positive.
questions.explanation: The professor says the return stroke begins once the upward streamer and the descending stepped leader connect.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention the Empire State Building?
options: To show that the return stroke moves upward from buildings
To explain why thunder sounds louder in large cities
To show that tall buildings protect the areas around them
To contradict a popular belief about where lightning strikes
questions.explanation: Being hit about twenty times a year disproves the saying that lightning never strikes the same place twice.

intro: Listen to a talk on a podcast about weather.
talk: Hey everyone. Today's story is about a river of wind, and a scientist the world almost forgot. In the nineteen twenties, a Japanese meteorologist named Wasaburo Ooishi ran an observatory north of Tokyo. He launched about thirteen hundred weather balloons and tracked them as they rose. He found that high up, around nine to twelve kilometers, a powerful wind blew steadily from west to east, far stronger than anything at the surface. He published his results in Esperanto, the international language he championed, and almost no one outside Japan read them. Then came the Second World War. Japan used Ooishi's findings to launch around nine thousand balloons carrying bombs toward North America, and some crossed the Pacific in about three days. At the same time, American bomber pilots flying high over Japan ran into headwinds of more than two hundred kilometers an hour, so strong their planes almost stood still over the ground. That's how the rest of the world discovered what we now call the jet stream. What drives it? The contrast between cold polar air and warm tropical air. Where they meet, the temperature difference creates a strong pressure difference high in the atmosphere, and the wind races along that boundary. That's why it's strongest in winter, when the contrast is greatest. Flights from New York to London are often an hour shorter than the return trip. But forecasters stress that it isn't a straight, steady river. It meanders in huge waves, and those bends steer storms.

questions.prompt: What is the podcast mainly about?
options: How Japanese weather balloons were used to measure winds near the surface
How a powerful high-altitude wind was discovered and what drives it
Why Ooishi chose to publish his scientific work in Esperanto
Why flights from London to New York take longer than expected
questions.explanation: The host tells how the jet stream was discovered and explains that it is driven by the contrast between polar and tropical air.

questions.prompt: Why did Ooishi's discovery go largely unnoticed at first?
options: His balloons failed to rise high enough to detect the strongest winds.
Japan kept his findings secret until the war had ended.
He reported it in a language few scientists outside Japan read.
Other scientists doubted the accuracy of his balloon data.
questions.explanation: The host says Ooishi published in Esperanto, so almost no one outside Japan read his results.

questions.prompt: What did Ooishi's balloons and the American bomber pilots' experiences have in common?
options: Both were used to carry bombs across the Pacific Ocean.
Both showed that the winds are strongest close to Earth's surface.
Both were reported in Esperanto after the war had ended.
Both revealed very strong westerly winds high in the atmosphere.
questions.explanation: Ooishi's balloons detected a strong west-to-east wind at high altitude, and the bombers met the same powerful wind over Japan.

questions.prompt: Why does the host mention flights between New York and London?
options: To give a familiar example of the jet stream's effect
To show that the jet stream blows from east to west
To explain how pilots first discovered the jet stream
To show that the jet stream is strongest in summer
questions.explanation: The shorter eastbound flight is an everyday example of the west-to-east jet stream helping travelers.

intro: Listen to a talk in an astronomy class.
talk: Every star eventually runs out of fuel. What's left afterward depends mostly on the star's mass. Take a star like our Sun. In about five billion years, it'll swell into a red giant, then gently shed its outer layers into space. What remains is the core, a white dwarf. A white dwarf packs about as much mass as the Sun into something the size of Earth. A teaspoonful would weigh tons. What keeps it from collapsing further? Not heat, but a quantum effect: electrons resist being squeezed into the same state, and that resistance holds the star up. Now, in nineteen thirty, a nineteen-year-old Indian student named Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar was on a ship sailing to England, and he worked out that this resistance has a limit. Above about one point four times the mass of the Sun, the electrons can't hold out, and gravity wins. That's the Chandrasekhar limit. Back then, though, the most famous astronomer in Britain, Arthur Eddington, publicly mocked the idea. He was sure nature wouldn't let a star collapse endlessly. So what happens to cores above the limit? They come from much heavier stars, roughly eight or more times the Sun's mass. Their cores collapse in under a second, triggering a supernova, and leave behind either a neutron star, only about twenty kilometers across, or, if heavy enough, a black hole. Chandrasekhar turned out to be right, and in nineteen eighty-three, more than fifty years later, he won the Nobel Prize for this work.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How white dwarfs gradually cool and turn into neutron stars
Why Eddington rejected the existence of red giants
How a star's mass determines what remains after it dies
How the Sun will eventually explode as a supernova
questions.explanation: The professor explains that a star's mass decides whether it ends as a white dwarf, a neutron star, or a black hole.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, what prevents a white dwarf from collapsing further?
options: Heat produced by continued fusion in its core
Gravity pulling its outer layers away from the core
Material it gains after shedding its outer layers
Electrons resisting being squeezed into the same state
questions.explanation: The professor says it is not heat but a quantum effect in which electrons resist being squeezed together.

questions.prompt: How does a white dwarf differ from a neutron star, according to the professor?
options: A white dwarf comes from a lighter star and is far larger in size.
A white dwarf comes from a heavier star and is far smaller in size.
A white dwarf forms in a supernova, but a neutron star does not.
A white dwarf is about twenty kilometers across, unlike a neutron star.
questions.explanation: White dwarfs come from Sun-like stars and are Earth-sized, while neutron stars come from much heavier stars and are about twenty kilometers across.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention Arthur Eddington?
options: To credit him with being the first to calculate the white dwarf mass limit
To show that Chandrasekhar's idea was at first dismissed by an authority
To explain why neutron stars are only twenty kilometers across
To show that he discovered the first known black hole
questions.explanation: Eddington, Britain's most famous astronomer, publicly mocked Chandrasekhar's limit, which was later proven correct.

intro: Listen to a talk in an astronomy class.
talk: In nineteen sixty-four, two radio astronomers at Bell Labs in New Jersey, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, had a problem with their antenna. It was a horn-shaped receiver built for satellite communication, and wherever they pointed it, they picked up a faint hiss of microwave noise. Day or night, every direction, the same. Naturally, they blamed the equipment. They even evicted nesting pigeons and scrubbed off what they politely called white dielectric material. The noise didn't change. Nearby, at Princeton, a team led by Robert Dicke was building an instrument to look for exactly this signal. Their reasoning: if the universe began in a hot, dense state, then about three hundred eighty thousand years later it would've cooled enough for atoms to form, and at that moment light could finally travel freely. That ancient light should still be everywhere, but stretched by the expansion of the universe into microwaves. Hearing the Bell Labs result, Dicke reportedly told his team, well, boys, we've been scooped. Why did this matter? At the time, the Big Bang had a serious rival, the steady-state theory, which said the universe had no beginning and always looked the same. That model had no natural way to produce a uniform glow at about three degrees above absolute zero. The Big Bang predicted it. Later satellites added a twist: the glow isn't perfectly uniform. It varies by about one part in a hundred thousand, and those tiny ripples were the seeds of galaxies.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How nesting pigeons interfered with early satellite communication systems
Why the steady-state theory predicted a uniform microwave glow
How a team at Princeton built the first horn-shaped antenna
The accidental discovery of radiation left over from the early universe
questions.explanation: The lecturer describes how Penzias and Wilson accidentally detected the leftover glow of the Big Bang.

questions.prompt: What did Penzias and Wilson first assume about the noise they detected?
options: It was caused by a problem with their equipment.
It came from a communication satellite overhead.
It was the signal predicted by the Big Bang theory.
It changed depending on the time of day.
questions.explanation: The lecturer says they naturally assumed the equipment was at fault and even cleaned out the pigeons' nest.

questions.prompt: What signal was Dicke's team preparing to search for, according to the lecturer?
options: Noise produced by birds nesting inside radio antennas
Light released when atoms formed, now stretched into microwaves
Microwaves released much later, when the first galaxies began forming
Light that varied greatly from one direction to another
questions.explanation: Dicke's team predicted that light freed when atoms formed would now fill the sky as microwaves, matching what Bell Labs had detected.

questions.prompt: Why does the lecturer mention the steady-state theory?
options: To identify the theory Penzias and Wilson set out to test
To explain why the glow varies by one part in a hundred thousand
To explain why the discovery strongly supported the Big Bang
To show that Dicke's team had rejected the Big Bang theory
questions.explanation: The steady-state theory could not explain a uniform microwave glow, while the Big Bang predicted it.

intro: Listen to a talk in a physics class.
talk: In eighteen twenty-seven, the Scottish botanist named Robert Brown was looking through his microscope at pollen grains suspended in water. Well, actually, at tiny particles that had come out of the pollen grains. And he noticed they were jiggling constantly, darting this way and that, never settling down. His first thought, natural for the time, was a life force, since the particles came from living plants. So he tested that idea. He examined pollen dried and stored for over a century. It jiggled. Then he tried things that had never been alive: powdered glass, ground-up rock, even dust from a fragment of the Sphinx. Everything small enough jiggled. So it wasn't life. We now call it Brownian motion. For nearly eighty years, nobody had a convincing answer. Remember, even in the late eighteen hundreds, some respected scientists doubted that atoms really existed. They saw them as a useful fiction for doing chemistry. Then, in nineteen oh five, Albert Einstein offered an explanation. A particle in water is constantly struck by water molecules from all sides. At any instant, slightly more hit one side than the other, so it gets nudged randomly. Einstein went further and predicted exactly how far a particle should drift over time. Three years later, a French physicist, Jean Perrin, carefully tracked particles under a microscope and found that Einstein's predictions matched. He could even estimate how many molecules a given amount of substance contains. After that, the doubters gave up. Atoms were real.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How a puzzling motion of tiny particles helped prove that atoms exist
How Robert Brown discovered that pollen grains are alive
Why particles from ground-up rocks move faster than particles from pollen
How Perrin disproved Einstein's predictions about molecules
questions.explanation: The professor traces Brownian motion from Brown's observation to Einstein's explanation and Perrin's confirmation that atoms are real.

questions.prompt: Why did Brown examine powdered glass and ground-up rock?
options: To compare their speed with that of particles from pollen
To see whether the motion required something that had been alive
To find particles small enough to be seen moving under a microscope
To show that only old pollen produced the jiggling motion
questions.explanation: Brown tested materials that had never been alive to check his idea that a life force caused the motion.

questions.prompt: What was Perrin's contribution, according to the professor?
options: He first observed particles jiggling in water under a microscope.
He proposed that molecules strike particles from all sides.
He confirmed Einstein's predictions by carefully tracking particles.
He showed the motion was caused by a life force in pollen.
questions.explanation: Perrin tracked particles under a microscope three years after Einstein's paper and found the predictions matched.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about the scientists who doubted atoms in the late eighteen hundreds?
options: They believed Brown's particles were driven by a kind of life force.
They rejected atoms because Brown's experiments with rock had failed.
They had already accepted that atoms existed before Einstein offered an explanation.
They were persuaded by the match between Einstein's theory and Perrin's data.
questions.explanation: The professor says the doubters gave up after Perrin's measurements confirmed Einstein's predictions.

intro: Listen to a talk in a physics class.
talk: In nineteen eleven, the Dutch physicist named Heike Kamerlingh Onnes was studying how metals behave at extremely low temperatures. He'd recently become the first to liquefy helium, which boils at about four degrees above absolute zero, so he could go colder than anyone before him. He cooled a thread of mercury, and as the temperature dropped, its electrical resistance did what you'd expect: it decreased gradually. Then, at about four point two kelvin, it didn't just get small. It vanished, all at once. He called it superconductivity. It really is zero. Current in a superconducting loop has flowed for years with no measurable loss. Then, in nineteen thirty-three, researchers found a second property. A superconductor pushes magnetic fields out of itself. That's called the Meissner effect, and it's why you can make a magnet float above one. For decades, the big limitation was temperature. Every known superconductor had to be cooled with expensive liquid helium, and many physicists believed the effect couldn't survive much above thirty kelvin. Then, in nineteen eighty-six, two researchers in Switzerland, Georg Bednorz and Alex Müller, found superconductivity in a ceramic, a copper oxide, at around thirty-five kelvin. Ceramics, materials usually thought of as poor conductors! Within a year, others found a related ceramic that worked at ninety-two kelvin. That's above seventy-seven kelvin, the boiling point of liquid nitrogen, which is about as cheap as milk. And here's the humbling part: almost forty years later, physicists still don't fully agree on why these ceramics work.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How Onnes became the first scientist to liquefy helium gas in his laboratory
The discovery of superconductivity and efforts to raise its temperature
Why magnets float above all metals at low temperatures
How liquid nitrogen is produced cheaply for laboratories
questions.explanation: The professor describes the discovery of superconductivity and the later discovery of ceramics that superconduct at higher temperatures.

questions.prompt: What surprised Onnes about mercury's resistance at about four point two kelvin?
options: It increased suddenly instead of continuing to fall gradually.
It decreased gradually, just as he had expected it would.
It disappeared suddenly instead of continuing to fall gradually.
It fell to zero only after several years of cooling.
questions.explanation: The professor says the resistance did not just get small but vanished all at once.

questions.prompt: Why was the ceramic found within a year of the Swiss discovery so significant?
options: It was the first material shown to have the Meissner effect.
It confirmed the thirty-kelvin limit that many physicists had expected.
It was the first copper oxide known to conduct electricity.
It could be cooled with liquid nitrogen rather than liquid helium.
questions.explanation: It worked at ninety-two kelvin, above the seventy-seven-kelvin boiling point of cheap liquid nitrogen, whereas earlier superconductors needed liquid helium.

questions.prompt: What is the professor's attitude toward the current understanding of ceramic superconductors?
options: He finds it humbling that they are still not fully explained.
He believes earlier theories already explain their behavior well.
He doubts that the ceramics are true superconductors.
He thinks they are too costly to be worth studying.
questions.explanation: He calls it humbling that physicists still do not fully agree on why the ceramics work.

intro: Listen to a talk in a chemistry class.
talk: By the eighteen sixties, chemists knew of about sixty-three elements, and several had noticed patterns. But it was the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev, in eighteen sixty-nine, who produced the table that stuck. He arranged the elements by atomic weight and grouped together those with similar chemical properties. Two bold decisions set his table apart. First, he left gaps. Where no known element fit, he didn't force one in; he said an undiscovered element belonged there, and he predicted its properties. For a gap below aluminum, he described an element he called eka-aluminum, with a density of about five point nine grams per cubic centimeter. In eighteen seventy-five, a French chemist discovered gallium, and it matched almost perfectly, except that he measured its density as four point seven. Mendeleev wrote back, essentially saying, your sample's impure, measure again. He did, and got five point nine. Second, Mendeleev occasionally broke his own rule. Tellurium is slightly heavier than iodine, but he put tellurium first, because iodine's properties clearly matched the next column. He assumed the atomic weights must be wrong. But the weights were right. The real explanation came in nineteen thirteen, when a young British physicist, Henry Moseley, used X-rays to show that each element has a characteristic number, the atomic number, which we now know is the number of protons. Ordered by atomic number, tellurium comes before iodine naturally. So the table's true organizing principle wasn't weight at all. Mendeleev had the right order for the wrong reason.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why gallium was the most difficult element for chemists to discover
How Moseley used X-rays to discover several new elements
How Mendeleev organized the elements and how his system was later explained
Why atomic weights were measured incorrectly by chemists in the eighteen sixties
questions.explanation: The lecturer explains Mendeleev's bold choices in his table and how Moseley's atomic numbers later explained them.

questions.prompt: What happened when gallium's density was first measured?
options: It matched Mendeleev's predicted value of four point seven exactly.
It showed that gallium belonged in a gap above aluminum.
It proved that Mendeleev had predicted the wrong density.
It differed from Mendeleev's prediction because the sample was impure.
questions.explanation: The first measurement was four point seven, but after Mendeleev said the sample was impure, it was remeasured at five point nine.

questions.prompt: Why did Mendeleev place tellurium before iodine?
options: Their chemical properties fit that order better than their weights did.
Tellurium had been measured with a slightly lower atomic weight than iodine.
Moseley's X-ray results showed that tellurium had fewer protons.
Iodine had not yet been discovered when he made his table.
questions.explanation: Mendeleev put tellurium first because iodine's properties matched the next column, even though tellurium is heavier.

questions.prompt: What does the lecturer mean when she says Mendeleev had the right order for the wrong reason?
options: His weights were correct, but his arrangement of the elements was not.
His arrangement was correct, but his belief about faulty weights was not.
His predictions were correct, but no one believed them at first.
His table was correct only for elements discovered after eighteen sixty-nine.
questions.explanation: Mendeleev's tellurium-iodine order was right, but the true reason was atomic number, not inaccurate weights.

intro: Listen to a talk on a podcast about the history of science.
talk: Welcome back. Today's story is about a tiny number that wouldn't go away. In the eighteen nineties, the English physicist Lord Rayleigh was precisely measuring the densities of gases, and noticed something odd about nitrogen. Nitrogen taken from the air, after removing oxygen, water, and carbon dioxide, was slightly heavier than nitrogen made from chemical compounds like ammonia, by about half a percent. Most people would've called that experimental error. Rayleigh didn't. He repeated the measurements, got the same gap, and wrote to the journal Nature asking readers to explain it. The chemist William Ramsay took up the challenge. His approach had three steps. First, he took nitrogen from the air. Second, he passed it repeatedly over hot magnesium, which reacts with nitrogen and removes it. Third, he examined what was left. About one percent of the gas refused to react. When he looked at its light through a spectroscope, he saw lines that matched no known element. They named it argon, from the Greek word for lazy. That created a headache: there was no place for it on the periodic table. The solution was an entirely new column, and within a few years Ramsay had found the rest of the family: helium, neon, krypton, and xenon. Both men won Nobel Prizes in nineteen oh four. Here's the twist. Back in seventeen eighty-five, Henry Cavendish had done a similar experiment and found a tiny bubble of air that wouldn't react. He recorded it, and nobody followed it up.

questions.prompt: What is the podcast mainly about?
options: Why nitrogen made from ammonia is heavier than the nitrogen taken from the air
How Henry Cavendish discovered argon in the eighteenth century
How Lord Rayleigh measured the density of helium and neon
How a small measurement difference led to the discovery of new elements
questions.explanation: The host explains how Rayleigh's half-percent density puzzle led Ramsay to discover argon and the other noble gases.

questions.prompt: What did Rayleigh notice about nitrogen taken from the air?
options: It was slightly denser than nitrogen made from chemical compounds.
It was slightly lighter than nitrogen made from ammonia.
It reacted more quickly with hot magnesium than Rayleigh had expected.
It still contained about one percent oxygen and water.
questions.explanation: The host says nitrogen from air was about half a percent heavier than nitrogen made from compounds like ammonia.

questions.prompt: In Ramsay's procedure, what was the purpose of the hot magnesium?
options: To remove the oxygen and water from the original air sample
To remove the nitrogen so that any other gas would be left over
To make the leftover gas react so its identity could be revealed
To produce pure nitrogen from compounds such as ammonia
questions.explanation: The magnesium reacted with and removed the nitrogen, leaving about one percent of an unreactive gas, argon.

questions.prompt: Why does the host mention Henry Cavendish?
options: To identify who first wrote to Nature about the nitrogen puzzle
To explain how Ramsay later found helium and neon
To point out that an earlier clue to argon had been overlooked
To show that Cavendish was the one who named argon
questions.explanation: Cavendish found an unreactive bubble of air over a century earlier, but nobody followed it up.

intro: Listen to a talk in a materials science class.
talk: Diamond and the graphite in your pencil are both pure carbon. Yet diamond is the hardest natural material known, and graphite is soft enough to mark paper. Why? It comes down to bonding. In diamond, every carbon atom is bonded to four neighbors, in a rigid three-dimensional network. There's no easy direction to break it. And since all of each atom's outer electrons are locked into bonds, diamond doesn't conduct electricity. In graphite, each carbon bonds to just three neighbors, forming flat sheets of hexagons, like chicken wire. The sheets are strong, but they're stacked loosely, held by weak forces, so they slide over each other. That's why graphite works as a lubricant, and why it rubs off onto paper. And because each atom has one electron left over, free to move, graphite conducts electricity. Here's a surprise. At normal surface conditions, graphite, not diamond, is the more stable form. A diamond is technically turning into graphite, just so slowly you'd never notice in a billion years. Now, what if you peeled graphite down to a single sheet, one atom thick? That's graphene. For decades, many physicists argued a sheet that thin would be unstable and crumple. Then, in two thousand four, two researchers in Manchester, Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov, made it using ordinary sticky tape, peeling layers off graphite again and again. Graphene turned out to be among the strongest materials ever tested, and it won them the Nobel Prize in twenty ten.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How the arrangement of carbon atoms determines a material's properties
Why diamonds very slowly turn into graphite under normal surface conditions
How graphite is processed to make pencils and lubricants
How physicists first predicted the strength of graphene
questions.explanation: The professor explains how different bonding arrangements give diamond, graphite, and graphene very different properties.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, why doesn't diamond conduct electricity?
options: Its atoms are arranged in flat, loosely stacked sheets.
All of its atoms' outer electrons are locked into bonds.
Each of its atoms has one free electron left over.
Its bonds break easily in one particular direction.
questions.explanation: The professor says diamond does not conduct because every outer electron is locked into a bond.

questions.prompt: How is graphene related to graphite, according to the professor?
options: It forms when graphite slowly changes into diamond.
It is a three-dimensional network of graphite's atoms.
It is a single sheet of the layers that make up graphite.
It is the weak force holding graphite's layers together.
questions.explanation: The professor describes graphene as graphite peeled down to a single sheet one atom thick.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention that physicists thought a single sheet would crumple?
options: To explain why graphene is weaker than diamond
To show why ordinary sticky tape could not produce graphene
To explain why graphite works well as a lubricant
To emphasize how unexpected the creation of graphene was
questions.explanation: The prediction that such a sheet would be unstable makes its simple creation with sticky tape more surprising.

intro: Listen to a talk in a materials science class.
talk: Why does an iron gate rust away while an aluminum ladder left outside for years looks fine? Both metals react with oxygen; the difference is what happens next. When iron reacts with oxygen and water, it forms rust, iron oxide, and rust is flaky and porous. It takes up more space than the original metal, so it cracks and falls off, exposing fresh iron underneath, and the process continues. Aluminum also forms an oxide, but it's a thin, tightly attached film that seals the surface, so oxygen can't reach the metal below. Engineers call this passivation. Stainless steel borrows aluminum's trick. In nineteen thirteen, in Sheffield, England, metallurgist Harry Brearley was seeking a gun-barrel steel that wouldn't wear away. As the story goes, he noticed that some rejected samples, thrown on a scrap pile, hadn't rusted. They contained a lot of chromium. Once steel has more than about ten and a half percent chromium, the chromium reacts with oxygen to form an invisible oxide layer only a few nanometers thick. Remarkably, if you scratch it, the layer re-forms within moments, as long as oxygen is around. It heals itself. But the name is a bit misleading. Stainless steel isn't stain-proof. Salt is its weakness. Chloride ions, in seawater or even swimming-pool air, can break through the film at tiny points and eat small, deep holes into the metal. That's called pitting. So for boats and coastal structures, engineers add another element, molybdenum, to toughen the film.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why aluminum is stronger than iron in outdoor structures
How a protective oxide layer keeps some metals from corroding
How Harry Brearley designed a new steel for making gun barrels
Why molybdenum is added to nearly every type of steel
questions.explanation: The lecturer explains how thin oxide films protect aluminum and stainless steel, unlike flaky rust on iron.

questions.prompt: According to the lecturer, why does rust allow iron to keep corroding?
options: It forms a thin, tight film that traps water on the metal.
It takes up less space than the iron, leaving small gaps.
It cracks and falls off, exposing fresh metal underneath.
It reacts with chromium in the air to form a new oxide.
questions.explanation: The lecturer says rust takes up more space than the iron, so it cracks and falls off and exposes fresh iron.

questions.prompt: How is stainless steel similar to aluminum?
options: Both contain at least ten and a half percent chromium.
Both form flaky oxides that fall off and then re-form.
Both resist the chloride ions that are found in seawater.
Both are protected by a thin oxide film that blocks oxygen.
questions.explanation: The lecturer says stainless steel borrows aluminum's trick of a thin, sealing oxide layer.

questions.prompt: What does the lecturer imply about the name stainless steel?
options: It overstates how well the metal resists every kind of corrosion.
It was chosen because Brearley's samples were completely stain-proof.
It accurately describes how the metal behaves in seawater.
It refers to the molybdenum added for use on boats.
questions.explanation: The lecturer calls the name misleading because chloride ions can still cause pitting corrosion.

intro: Listen to a talk in a structural engineering class.
talk: On November seventh, nineteen forty, the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State twisted itself apart in a wind of only about sixty-five kilometers an hour. Open for just four months, it was a suspension bridge with a main span of over eight hundred meters, but its deck was unusually thin and narrow, only about two point four meters deep, much shallower than earlier designs. That made it elegant and cheap, but flexible. Even in light winds, the deck rose and fell in waves, so much that locals nicknamed it Galloping Gertie, and people drove across it for the thrill. On the final morning, though, the motion changed. After a cable connection slipped, the deck stopped simply moving up and down and started twisting, one side rising as the other fell. Within about an hour, the center span tore loose and fell. For decades, physics textbooks called this the classic example of resonance: the idea that the wind pushed at exactly the bridge's natural frequency, like a child being pushed on a swing. But engineers point out a problem: a steady wind doesn't push in rhythm. The accepted explanation now is aeroelastic flutter. As the deck twisted, its changing angle altered how the wind struck it, and that pushed it to twist even further. The motion fed itself, drawing more and more energy from a steady wind. Today, models of major bridges are tested in wind tunnels, and the replacement bridge was built with a much deeper, stiffer deck.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How engineers designed a deeper, stiffer bridge deck to resist very strong winds
Why thin bridge decks are cheaper to build than deep ones
Why a suspension bridge collapsed and how that collapse is now explained
How wind tunnels were first invented to test bridge models
questions.explanation: The professor describes the Tacoma Narrows collapse and why flutter, not simple resonance, is now the accepted explanation.

questions.prompt: What does the professor say about the bridge's deck?
options: It was deeper and stiffer than earlier bridge designs.
It was designed after testing models in wind tunnels.
It moved only during unusually strong winds.
It was much shallower than the decks of earlier bridges.
questions.explanation: The professor says the deck was only about two point four meters deep, much shallower than earlier designs.

questions.prompt: How did the bridge's motion on the final morning differ from its usual motion?
options: The deck began twisting instead of only rising and falling.
The deck began rising and falling instead of twisting.
The deck stopped moving after a cable connection slipped.
The deck moved up and down for the very first time.
questions.explanation: The deck normally rose and fell in waves, but after a cable connection slipped it started twisting.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention a child being pushed on a swing?
options: To show how a steady wind can produce regular, rhythmic pushes
To illustrate an explanation that is now considered inadequate
To explain the current theory of aeroelastic flutter
To describe how drivers enjoyed crossing the bridge
questions.explanation: The swing illustrates the textbook resonance explanation, which engineers now reject because a steady wind does not push in rhythm.

intro: Listen to a talk in an aerospace engineering class.
talk: How does a wing produce lift? You've probably heard this. The wing's top is curved and its bottom flat, so air over the top travels farther. Since the air above and below has to meet again at the back edge at the same time, the top air must go faster, and faster air has lower pressure, so the wing is pushed up. It's in many textbooks, and its key step is wrong. There's no physical law saying the two streams have to meet at the back. In wind tunnels with puffs of smoke, the air over the top actually arrives well before the air underneath. So the top air is faster, much faster than predicted, but not for that reason. Two cases defeat the textbook version. First, stunt planes can fly upside down, with the curved side facing the ground. Second, a paper airplane has completely flat wings, and it flies fine. So what's going on? The key is the angle of attack, the angle between the wing and the oncoming air. A wing tilted slightly upward, helped by its curved shape, turns the airflow downward. If the wing pushes air down, the air pushes the wing up. That's Newton's third law. The pressure difference is just another description of the same flow. More angle gives more lift, but only up to a point. At around fifteen degrees, the air can no longer follow the top surface. It breaks away, lift drops suddenly, and the wing stalls.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How stunt planes are specially designed to fly upside down
Why faster-moving air always produces higher pressure
How wind tunnels with smoke are used to measure the speed of airplanes
Why a common explanation of lift is wrong and what really causes it
questions.explanation: The lecturer rejects the equal-path explanation of lift and explains lift in terms of angle of attack and downward-turned air.

questions.prompt: According to the lecturer, what did wind-tunnel tests with smoke reveal?
options: Air over the top of the wing reaches the back edge first.
Air above and below the wing reaches the back edge together.
Air under the wing moves faster than air over the top.
Air over the top moves more slowly than textbooks predict.
questions.explanation: The lecturer says the smoke shows air over the top arriving well before the air underneath.

questions.prompt: What point does the lecturer make with stunt planes and paper airplanes?
options: Both rely on wings that are curved on top and completely flat underneath.
Both fly in ways the common textbook explanation cannot account for.
Both stall when their wings are tilted at very small angles.
Both produce lift mainly from faster air beneath the wing.
questions.explanation: Upside-down flight and flat paper wings both contradict the idea that lift depends on a curved top and longer path.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about a wing tilted at twenty degrees?
options: It produces more lift than the same wing tilted at ten degrees.
It forces the air above and below to meet at the back edge.
It is likely to lose lift because air separates from its surface.
It turns the airflow downward better than at any other angle.
questions.explanation: The lecturer says that at around fifteen degrees the air breaks away and the wing stalls, so twenty degrees would be past that point.

intro: Listen to a talk in a computer science class.
talk: In the late nineteen forties, the mathematician Richard Hamming, at Bell Labs, could use an early relay computer only on weekends. The machine could detect errors, but all it could do was abandon the job and move on. Hamming came back two weekends in a row to find his work dumped. He asked, essentially, if the machine can tell something's wrong, why can't it tell where, and fix it? The standard trick then was a parity bit. You add one extra bit so the total number of ones is always even. If a single bit flips, the count becomes odd, and you know there's an error. But you don't know which bit. Another option was sending every bit three times and take a majority vote. That does correct errors, but it triples the amount of data. Hamming found a middle path. In his best-known code, you take four bits of data and add three parity bits, so seven in total. The trick is that each parity bit checks a different, overlapping group of positions. When a bit flips, some checks fail and others pass, and that pattern of failures spells out, in binary, the exact position of the bad bit. Flip it back, and the error's corrected. Published in nineteen fifty, versions of it still protect computer memory. Now, Hamming's code fixes only one error at a time. Modern codes, like those in QR codes, can recover data even when about thirty percent of the symbol is damaged.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How a method was developed to locate and correct errors in data
Why early computers were available to researchers only on weekends
How parity bits double the amount of data that is transmitted
Why QR codes are more easily damaged than computer memory
questions.explanation: The professor explains how Hamming moved beyond error detection to a code that finds and corrects a flipped bit.

questions.prompt: What frustrated Hamming about the computer he used?
options: It failed to detect errors made by its relays.
It detected errors but simply abandoned the job.
It corrected errors but took the whole weekend.
It sent each bit three times and ran too slowly.
questions.explanation: The professor says the machine noticed errors but could only drop the job and move on.

questions.prompt: How does Hamming's seven-bit code compare with sending each bit three times?
options: Both can detect an error, but neither can locate the flipped bit.
Hamming's code triples the data, while repetition adds three bits.
Both can correct an error, but Hamming's code adds fewer extra bits.
Repetition corrects more errors because it relies on parity checks.
questions.explanation: Repetition corrects errors but triples the data, while Hamming's code corrects one error by adding just three bits to four.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention QR codes at the end of the talk?
options: To give an example of where Hamming's original code is used today
To explain how parity bits are arranged in overlapping groups
To show that QR codes can correct only one error at a time
To show that newer codes can handle much more damage than Hamming's
questions.explanation: The professor contrasts Hamming's single-error correction with modern codes that recover data despite about thirty percent damage.

intro: Listen to a talk on a podcast about technology.
talk: Hi everyone. Today: packet switching, the idea that makes the internet work. Start with the old telephone network. A call got a dedicated circuit, a continuous connection reserved for the whole call, even during long silences. That's called circuit switching, and for voice, it works. But computers don't talk like people. They send data in short bursts with long gaps, so a reserved line would sit idle most of the time. In the early nineteen sixties, an engineer at the RAND Corporation, Paul Baran, proposed something different. A few years later, Donald Davies in Britain came up with nearly the same idea independently, and he's the one who coined the word packet. Here's how it works. First, a message is broken into small pieces, each labeled with its destination. Second, each piece travels through the network on its own, and two pieces of the same message might take completely different routes. Third, the receiving computer puts them back in order. If a link fails, packets simply go around it. Telephone engineers were skeptical; one reportedly told Baran it wouldn't work. But in nineteen sixty-nine, the ARPANET sent its first message, from UCLA to a research institute in northern California. They tried to type the word login. The system crashed after two letters, L and O. You've probably heard the ARPANET was built to survive a nuclear war. That was Baran's motivation, yes. But the people who funded ARPANET mainly wanted researchers to share expensive computers.

questions.prompt: What is the podcast mainly about?
options: Why telephone calls require a dedicated circuit to be reserved for them
How data is sent across networks in small, separately routed pieces
How the ARPANET was designed mainly to survive a nuclear war
Why early computers crashed when they sent long messages
questions.explanation: The host explains packet switching, contrasts it with circuit switching, and describes its early history.

questions.prompt: According to the host, why was circuit switching poorly suited to computers?
options: Computers need several circuits reserved at once to send their long messages.
Computer data was too large to fit on one telephone circuit.
Computers send data in bursts, so a reserved line would often sit idle.
Computers could not send any data during long silences.
questions.explanation: The host says computers send short bursts with long gaps, so a dedicated line would be idle most of the time.

questions.prompt: According to the host, what happens after the packets travel through the network?
options: The receiving computer labels each one with its destination.
They are combined into a single circuit for the return trip.
They are broken into smaller pieces for each separate route.
The receiving computer puts them back in the correct order.
questions.explanation: The host lists breaking and labeling first, independent travel second, and reassembly by the receiver third.

questions.prompt: What is the host's point about the claim that ARPANET was built to survive a nuclear war?
options: It confuses Baran's goal with the main reason ARPANET was funded.
It is accurate because Baran personally designed and built the ARPANET.
It explains why the first message crashed after two letters.
It shows that telephone engineers supported packet switching.
questions.explanation: The host says survival was Baran's motivation, but ARPANET's funders mainly wanted researchers to share computers.
